comments.text: 51:01 I still don't fully understand what world models are if not this. Essentially, you want to use very specific algorithms to assign the original data that was ingested to broader concepts in the world and have it extrapolate/associate tokens based on that rather than reinforcement learning? Essentially substituting abstraction for human feedback. It sounds limiting though because humans aren't like that. We take in both and use both to reinforce/refine our heuristics into broader concepts. It seems like the reinforcement learning is always going to be the basis of any subsequent higher-concept associations being hardwired into the model no matter what. There might be a lot of excess reinforcement learning that is being pruned, but isn't there always going to be some sort of fundamental "core memory* (like inside out, but keep in mind that that creator did a bunch of research for his movie) reinforcement that is needed to build more abstract associations?

comments.author: @pmiddlet72
comments.text:
As far as reasoning is concerned with some thing we think that reasons (an anthropomorphism) - this is neither necessarily provable nor disprovable given what agreement (or lack thereof)  there is on what reasoning by its essence is.. In the cog sci world, 'intelligence', 'reasoning', 'thinking', are all terms that end up being headings for hierarchical properties. Any of these are emergent properties of more atomistic properties of a 'brain' (in vivo or in silico). Trying to prove an emergent property, which is an abstraction, of some thing, is within the scope of difficulty of understanding 'the black box' (in which we've more recently begun to innovate ways of 'probing'). 

Joe's absolutely right, because all of these things operate under laws of probability, RL won't eliminate bad answers. It also may have a theoretical limit on what accuracy can be attained by its use - we don't quite know what that is, at least yet. This assumes that what we're feeding a model is theoretically 'high quality'. At the very least, and given whether the current transformer architectures or future one's will help, I do think much higher accuracy (with non-zero probability of error, even big errors) is achievable. But this is a logarithmic exercise (i.e. we'll hit 'diminishing returns' in fits and spats, and eventually the work and energy to alter the ROC curve at smaller and smaller scales may make further attempts to make accuracy better on tasks of a wide spectrum in complexity likely infeasible - in my mind, at least in the foreseeable future).
